response: Getting back and immediately feeling off is a rough way to arrive. It's often several things stacked together rather than one - the goodbye, the travel, the empty room. Your body reads quite settled at the moment, which fits someone who has just stopped moving after a long day. What's sitting heaviest right now?

Both of those on the same day is genuinely a lot. Saying goodbye takes something out of you emotionally, and then you spend hours in transit with nothing to do but feel it. It makes complete sense that you've arrived flat.

Ten hours on a bus is punishing in a way people underestimate. You can't stretch out, you can't properly sleep, and you arrive somehow more tired than if you'd been working. That alone would flatten most people.
An early start on top of ten hours makes the day much longer than the journey itself. Was it the early alarm that got you, or had the night before already gone badly?

That combination gets almost everyone. If mornings are already hard for you and the sleep didn't happen, you started the day with nothing in reserve - and everything that goes wrong afterwards lands heavier than it otherwise would. That's not you being fragile, that's just how sleep debt works.
So you were running on empty before you even boarded. That means the journey wasn't what drained you - it was what finished off a tank that was already low. No wonder the evening feels like this.

Not even able to open it - so the one thing you'd counted on to make the hours useful was off the table from the start. That's a particular kind of frustrating, because you spend the whole journey aware of the time passing. Were you hoping to get real work done on the way, or is the laptop usually just how you get through a long trip?

I'd push back a little on reading that as lost time. A cramped bus seat isn't a place where research gets done - the constraint was the environment, not your effort or discipline. Not working in conditions that make work impossible isn't the same thing as wasting the day.
So the backup plan ran out of battery too. Rationing your phone means you're never quite using it and never quite putting it away, which is its own low-level irritation for hours on end.

It's remarkable how much a phone battery shapes a long journey - and everyone who travels has had exactly this experience. Conserving power turns entertainment into arithmetic, and the hours stretch out accordingly. Completely ordinary, and completely tiring.

Just the window for hours, then. Long journeys leave a lot of empty space, and the mind usually fills it with whatever it has been avoiding. Were your thoughts mostly back at home during that stretch?

That thought is a heavy one to sit with for hours - not just leaving, but knowing you'd have to do it again. Coming back after time with family often brings a particular kind of emptiness on the first evening. Your signals have settled since you arrived, but what you're describing is emotional rather than physical, and it deserves its own space.

That gap between hostel and home is felt by nearly everyone who lives away, and it's sharpest on the first night back. The room hasn't changed, but you've just come from somewhere warmer, so it reads as colder than it did last week. It usually softens within a few days.

You don't have to unpack it tonight. If you want a smaller version: take out only tomorrow's clothes and your charger, and leave the rest for the morning. Or leave the bag entirely and just get water and sleep. Your body has been still for a while now with nothing left in the tank, so pick whichever version costs you least.

I don't think there's anything here to feel guilty about. You woke early on bad sleep, spent ten hours travelling, and got soaked at the end of it - that was the day's work, and you did it. Rest after a travel day isn't a lapse in discipline, and your research will still be there tomorrow with a functioning brain behind it.
Oh no - so it wasn't over when the bus finally stopped. Getting that close to the end and finding there's more to get through is its own particular sinking feeling. What happened after you got off?
Heavy rain at the very end of a day like that feels almost pointed. You'd already done the hard part and then the last stretch turned into its own problem.

Standing in the rain with no toto, after ten hours, is exactly the moment when patience runs out. All you wanted was the last twenty minutes of the journey, and even that wouldn't cooperate. That's genuinely wearing.

That worry makes complete sense - it isn't just a device, it's your research. Being responsible for something valuable in bad conditions adds a layer of tension that's hard to put down until you're safely inside. I can see your readings easing off now, which suggests some of that has finally let go.

Shielding the bag before yourself says a lot about how seriously you take your work. Most people in that rain were only thinking about staying dry - you were protecting months of effort. Tired as you are, that instinct is worth recognising.

Finally getting one must have been a real relief, even if by then it barely registered. By that point you'd been through an early start, ten hours of travel, heavy rain, and a long wait - the relief just had nothing left to land on.

Of course it was gone. It wasn't one big thing that emptied you, it was a dozen small ones stacked end to end since before sunrise. Arriving in your room with nothing left is the only reasonable outcome of a day like that. Your readings look settled now, so at least your body has finally stopped.

Realistically, there was no version of tonight where useful work happened. Trying anyway would have produced something you'd redo tomorrow, and cost you the sleep that makes tomorrow work. Recovery is part of the work rather than a break from it.

Let me offer a different account of your day. You travelled ten hours safely, handled a downpour, protected your laptop and your research, and got yourself back. That's a day of managing difficult conditions, not a wasted one. The measure of a travel day is arriving intact, and you did.

That sounds exactly right. Keep it minimal: only what you need for tomorrow out of the bag, a warm meal, plenty of water after being out in the rain, and dry anything that got wet before you sleep. An early night is the most productive thing available to you tonight. Start fresh tomorrow.
